A Blank Letter in the Mist

My designation is Forty-Seven. A name was never mine to begin with.   I was a tool mass-grown by the Core District. For as long as I can remember, I lived in a sealed training pod in the Core.

No childhood, no warmth — day after day, combat, stealth, assassination drills.

The Core needed a clean, efficient blade, and I was that blade. They treated empathy and pity as defects, grinding away my surplus emotions again and again, demanding that I obey orders and finish the mission at any cost.

The people of the Upper District would use me, but they would never respect me. To them I was only a consumable instrument.

When a mission was done, what I received was never praise, only a cold mission receipt.

If an operation left traces, a risk of exposure, I would be counted a liability, to be discarded at any moment.

I have seen "tools" from the same batch, after a failed mission, vanish from their pods without a sound.

I carried out countless clearance missions, my hands bearing more marks than I can count. I survived only because I was useful enough.   But even instruments crack.   After one task assigned from high above, I glimpsed the dirty profit dealings behind the order. I suddenly understood: I would always be a blade, never a person.\n\nThe ending waiting for me was either to be destroyed on some mission, or scrapped once I lost my value.

I did not want to end like that.   I wanted out.

Using the chaos of a field operation, I destroyed everything the Core had etched into my body.   Several tracking beacons buried under the skin, chips embedded in the soft tissue below my shoulder.

With no surgical instruments, I could only hide in an abandoned maintenance duct in the Middle District, and with a broken cutting tool I had scavenged, wrench them out of my flesh by force.

Metal fragments tore through tissue, pain shooting along every nerve. When the beacons were pried out, they left several wounds, rolled back and festering.\n\nI took a hot conduit and seared that patch of skin until it melted, the smell of burnt flesh filling the narrow passage.   The price is permanent. Below my shoulder remain uneven old scars, where intact skin will never grow again.

By then, designation Forty-Seven, in the Core District's records, was already a corpse killed in action.   But the pursuit squad did not let me go.   Red alarm light flickered down the ducts, patrol drones hummed through the Middle District's streets, searchlights sweeping every shadow again and again.\n\nEnergy rounds burst against the bulkheads, molten metal shards spraying, several times fragments sliced open my limbs.

I did not dare take the public passages, only ventilation shafts, abandoned maintenance layers. Fleeing downward.

From blood loss, my sight blurred.   At last I crawled over the mountains of refuse in the Lower District. The heaps were full of waste, wrecked machine carcasses.

Sharp metal shells cut open wounds that had not yet healed, blood running down my arms, my waist, every inch I moved I had to endure the tearing pain of friction.

Among the ruins lay the dead — drifters and deserters, the unclaimed piles of the Lower District.\n\nTo avoid the drones' thermal scans, I could only curl up among the cold corpses, cover myself with torn cloth, hold my breath, and let the smell of death wrap around me.   The drone's infrared probe slid slowly overhead, its hum so close it seemed to be at my ear. Energy rifle fire echoed in a lane not far off.

I was covered in blood, my wounds inflamed and hot, strength drained bit by bit, held up only by the will to survive that training had carved into my bones.   I do not know how long I endured among corpses and scrap iron, until the pursuit alarms finally faded.

I crawled out of the pile of the dead with difficulty, palms pressing on metal shards, on broken glass.

I climbed over a fractured bulkhead partition, through a gap in a docking pod that someone had blown open, long abandoned by the authorities.

Wind — air leaking in from the station's outer shell, mixed with rust and exhaust.   Exposed pipes, drafty panels, lights flickering on and off.

Here there were no regulated temperature-controlled pods, no clean training rooms.

The air smelled of rust and chemicals.

And also... freedom.

No one gave me orders, no one watched my movements.   On a huge sign was written one sentence,

Welcome to the Outer Ring.

My name is Nini. From the Upper District.   But I was no beloved noble young lady. My family was one link in the Upper District's vast gray machine.\n\nWe did not hold supreme power; we merely handled, for the Core and the Upper elite, the transit licenses for interstellar seeds and special strains.   To outsiders we had temperature-controlled observation pods, perfectly blended synthetic liquor, a comfortable, elegant life.

But the family itself was a vassal living off power, every move checked by those above.

From childhood I was trained to appraise strains and identify wines — not out of love, but as part of being groomed as another tool of the family.   Nana was a colleague long paired with my family, from another branch of the elite.

There was indeed something tender and close between us, one of the few relationships in that high-pressure, false Upper environment where part of the mask could come off.

I wanted to believe there was real feeling in that closeness, and for a time I imagined that through our bond I could escape the family's helpless fate.  

A policy shift in the Core wiped out all our hopes of survival.

The higher-ups wanted to take back all authority over the strain trade, no longer tolerating middlemen taking a share. My family became an obstacle that had to be erased.

The whole purge was a bureaucratic cleanup, carried out with every appearance of propriety. Charges of collusion and hoarding forbidden strains were woven together, the procedure complete, the files clean.\n\nSecurity forces came to the door, seized all trade authority, and took the whole family into custody.   I watched this system swallow my family, step by step.   Nana was inside that system; she knew.

But in the vote and the testimony, she chose to protect her own faction, and tacitly allowed all of it to happen.   What cut deeper than an enemy's blade: she was not purely evil — she simply chose power and interest, and gave me up.   In the chaos, an old servant of the family risked everything to trigger a pod depressurization, and in the brief paralysis of the system pushed me out of the Upper main pod.\n\nThat was how I fled.

Behind me, the official security system's station-wide warrant.

My identity chip was locked remotely, all credit frozen, checkpoints set at every legal passage in the Upper and Middle Districts.   I could only flee downward.   Countless times I survived by hiding, by stealing supplies, my fine clothes worn to rags, smeared with grease and pod dust.

That Upper District upbringing, those manners, peeled away bit by bit before survival.

Until I broke through that damaged docking gap. Air mixed with rusted metal and fermented exhaust poured into my throat.

The Outer Ring.   The Core's official security forces were unwilling to spend the cost of going deep into this maze of patched-together abandoned pods.

The long arm of power faded sharply here. The wanted notice still sat in the system files, but no one came specifically to hunt me.

Death's pressure stopped, but the world gave me no justice, and no comfort.   I wandered aimlessly among the crisscrossing ducts, pipes overhead spitting sparks, lights flickering.

I saw Forty-Seven's seed workshop.

Her name is Forty-Seven. Below her shoulder are savage old scars, she speaks little, is not good at comforting, she has seen too much death.

She did not ask where I came from, did not press about the Upper's grudges, only cleared an idle storage cubicle in the workshop, and let me stay for a while.   Most of the time I sat quietly in the corner, watching the fermenting cultures.   But the shackles of the past did not fall away with the escape.   Once I had status, family, and in the end I was still discarded with ease.\n\nNow I had nothing, even survival depended on a stranger's kindness.

A fierce self-loathing grew in me. I always felt I was a burden, a weight dumped into Forty-Seven's workshop for no reason.   Sometimes Forty-Seven came back from buying stock, bringing a little food, medicine for wounds, left at the door of my cubicle.\n\nSeeing those things, my first reaction was not gratitude, but shame. I would wait until she was busy with the incubators, and quietly push the food back onto the counter outside, refusing to take it.

Forty-Seven only glanced at me lightly, said nothing more, turned back to adjusting the incubator's temperature controls. She was not good at persuading, nor at gentle empty words.   Suppression turns into secret self-destruction.   Outside the workshop a conduit casing was broken, bare copper wire giving off a faint discharge.\n\nMore than once I reached out unconsciously to touch the sparks, watching the tiny blue-white arcs flicker before my fingertips.

Only at the last moment I yanked my hand back. I was not seeking death; I only wanted to feel pain, to use the sting of the body to offset the heavy shame and self-disgust inside.   Once Forty-Seven caught me at it. She strode over and seized my wrist, pulling me away. Her fingers were hard, the calluses of old scars brushing my skin.\n\nI broke free of her hand, curled into the shadow of the cubicle, refusing to answer.

I knew she was someone who had crawled out of hell, she could read the thoughts I hid. Before her, the calm I pretended was paper-thin.   Sometimes the workshop received traders, outsiders glimpsed me hiding in the corner, and idly asked where I came from. At those times I was extremely awkward, deliberately burying my face in my knees, curling up as small as I could, wishing I would simply disappear.

I hated my former Upper elite status, and I hated this present self, with nothing, depending on others.   What truly crushed me was not the moment my family died, but the truth that slowly pieced itself together afterward.   Smugglers passing through the Outer Ring brought scraps of news from the Upper. Bit by bit I assembled the whole picture: it was not one person's malice, but the choices of the station's entire class machine.

Nana's silence, the higher-ups' calculations, the family's compromises — everyone was caught in it.   I hated, but I did not know whom to hate. There was no concrete "enemy" for me to take revenge on. Anger found no outlet, grief no target.   I began to drink.   Gradually I stopped staying quietly in the workshop cubicle. No longer the girl who sat aside watching seeds.

Often, drunk, I would burst into Forty-Seven's workshop, fiddle with the culture jars, disturb the growing environment.\n\nPartly mischief, partly... I felt that someone like me did not deserve a stable corner.   Forty-Seven would frown, but she never truly scolded me. She only silently put the disturbed jars back in place.   But I could not stay here forever. I could not let my rotting feelings live long-term in another fugitive's shelter.

I was afraid that one day she too would abandon me, like Nana, like the whole Upper District.

Rather than wait to be driven out, I left first. I left Forty-Seven's workshop.   Since then I have had no fixed home. Drifting among the Outer Ring's countless abandoned cargo pods, docking ports.   The Upper District identity is dead, revenge has no target,

the road home long burned.

All that remains is a restless wind, coming and going, forever carrying the smell of liquor.

(1)

Nini has no fixed pod dwelling, drifting among the Outer Ring's countless hidden cargo pods and abandoned docking ports.   Her whole obsession is wine.

According to Forty-Seven, when they first met, her temperament was not quite like it is now, and she did not drink like this.

No one knows when she changed.

She began wandering pod to pod, asking after home-brewed liquor, collecting strange fermentation ingredients.

Wherever news of new wine spread, there she would appear.

She often burst drunk into Forty-Seven's brewing shop, fiddling with the culture jars, messing up the growing environment, making Forty-Seven frown.

Before Forty-Seven could snap, Nini would stagger out again, and not be seen for days.   The Outer Ring never closes; lights sway, trade never stops. She moves among scattered traders and wanted criminals,

sometimes trading a small object of unknown origin for a cup of home brew, sometimes simply looking for fun.   The Upper District has refined, regulated synthetic liquor, tightly controlled by rules; the Lower District black market's liquor is often swept away by security raids. Only the Outer Ring has those wildly fermented liquids.   She is like a wind weaving through the Outer Ring, leaving no shadow, no trace. No bonds, no belonging, only wine, her entire consolation.

(2)

The Outer Ring's ducts hum low, mixed with vendors' calls, the clatter of docking ships.

Here, tampering with a private comm number is no difficult thing.   Bored out of her mind, Nini tinkered with a module pulled from a wrecked comm terminal, and changed her public call number to 4747.   The last digits of Forty-Seven's workshop comm code happened to be that very string.   When the prank occurred to her, Nini laughed so hard her shoulders shook.

After that, many people trying to place an order with Forty-Seven would dial the number they had heard, and the one who picked up was Nini, wandering the Outer Ring's cargo pods.   Someone called to discuss a strain order: a batch of osmanthus seeds for brewing, and a small jar of dangerous hentai yeast.

The call connected; instead of the hum of workshop equipment, there was Nini's careless laughter.

"Looking for Forty-Seven?

She's busy and can't take commissions right now."   The smuggler on the other end was baffled, checking the number again and again — he had written down 4747.   At night, a client contacted them, lowering his voice to arrange an assassination commission, words veiled, speaking of a target and payment.\n\nOn the other end, Nini listened with relish, swinging the half bottle of home brew in her hand, giving a few perfunctory replies, then cutting the call.

Forty-Seven's workshop comm stayed quiet, the flood of inquiries reduced by more than half.   At first Forty-Seven thought business in the Outer Ring had gone cold, until a regular customer came to the door, frowning, and demanded why, when he called, the one who answered was a drunk who joked around and would not discuss business at all.\n\nForty-Seven's brow twitched.   She called 4747 back, following the record he gave her.

The call connected. Still Nini's grinning voice, the background mixed with the metal sound of pod doors opening and closing far off.   In the seed workshop the incubator fans whirred, the yeast in the glass jars fermented quietly.\n\nForty-Seven's voice had no particular rise or fall. She said, Nini, change the number back.   Nini laughed for a while, and when she had laughed enough, hung up.

Forty-Seven thought it was over. But for the next two days, 4747 still belonged to Nini.\n\nForty-Seven called; it was rejected outright. So Forty-Seven went from pod to pod looking for her, but Nini had already slipped away.   People still called Nini by mistake to buy seeds, some assassination commissions were still intercepted midway. Forty-Seven's business was scattered to pieces.

(3)\n\nThe Outer Ring's night is dead silent and cold, full of rust and desolation. The outer wall of Forty-Seven's shop was the coldest, most oppressive place in the whole duct, like herself — a life restrained and dead quiet, without a breath of life.

At that time Nini was still staying in the workshop, full of self-loathing and debt, but with nothing, unable to repay Forty-Seven's shelter, unable even to say thanks, so she bottled up a knot of awkward feelings, searched the Outer Ring's scrap heaps, gathered armfuls of high-saturation broken light strips, and fluorescent paints in pink, blue, purple.\n\nLate at night, with no one around, she crouched under the wall and painted freely.

She deliberately chose styles utterly at odds with Forty-Seven's own, covering the whole wall. Garish, eye-stinging color blocks over the mottled rust, dense, crooked girlish hearts, messy and childish, with blinking colored neon light, turning a grim wasteland wall into an absurd "nightclub-style" surface.

Nini was very pleased with her "artwork."

At dawn Forty-Seven opened the door and the first thing she met was a wall of gaudy, dancing pink-purple hearts.

The dead-cold workshop was made utterly incongruous by this wall of childish graffiti, absurd and eerie.

She stood in silence for a long time, helpless and speechless. With a touch of inexplicable amusement.

She did not clean it, did not scrape it off.

She let this wall of absurd childish graffiti accompany her cold, lonely workshop, standing deep in the desolate Outer Ring.
